title: Research Bits: Sept. 1
gist: Three gallium nitride results push GaN power and RF electronics past long-standing limits: EPFL's intrinsic polarization superjunction transistor on low-cost silicon withstands nearly 4 kV versus the ~600-650 V breakdown of conventional GaN devices while keeping low resistance and needing no chemical doping; a Nagoya/MIT/Cornell-led team hits (1-3) x 10^-4 ohm-cm^2 p-GaN contact resistivity using an ultrathin magnesium layer annealed at 600C for five minutes; and MIT, Georgia Tech and Penn State embed GaN dielets in a single-crystal diamond interposer to build a 4 W power amplifier whose thermal equalization improves rather than degrades performance.

insights.claim: EPFL's intrinsic polarization superjunction GaN transistor withstands nearly 4 kilovolts before breaking down while maintaining low resistance, against conventional GaN transistors that break down at around 600-650 V.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: A roughly six-fold breakdown improvement would put GaN into voltage classes currently owned by silicon carbide and silicon IGBTs — the key threshold for GaN to attack grid, industrial and EV traction markets.
insights.quote: the iPSJ can withstand nearly 4 kilovolts (kV) before breaking down, which the team claims is a record for this type of technology, while maintaining low resistance

insights.claim: The EPFL device is built from GaN layers on a low-cost silicon base rather than an exotic substrate, keeping the high-voltage result on a manufacturable and cheap platform.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: GaN-on-Si economics plus SiC-class voltage handling is the combination that would compress silicon carbide's cost premium in high-voltage power conversion.
insights.quote: Made from layers of GaN on a low-cost silicon base

insights.claim: The mechanism is engineering GaN layers to form a sheet of positive charge alongside the electron sheet and tuning material thickness so the two charge sheets balance throughout the device, letting voltage spread evenly along the transistor length at turn-off — and it eliminates the need for chemical doping.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Removing the doping step simplifies process flow and removes a variability source, which matters more than raw device physics for volume manufacturing cost.
insights.quote: The approach also eliminates the need for chemical doping.
insights.locator: The transistor's GaN layers are engineered

insights.claim: EPFL's POWERlab head Elison Matioli frames the next objective as combining approaches to solve the twin challenges of next-generation power electronics — handling very high voltages safely while minimizing resistance and the resulting energy loss — indicating the two goals have so far been traded off against each other.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: The voltage-versus-on-resistance tradeoff is the fundamental metric on which GaN, SiC and silicon power devices compete; watch it as the scoreboard for wide-bandgap displacement.
insights.quote: the twin challenges facing next-generation power electronics: handling very high voltages safely, while minimizing electrical resistance and the resulting energy loss

insights.claim: EPFL positions the device for EVs and industrial power systems specifically because it holds high voltage across a wide temperature range, where electronics must operate reliably under high temperature and electrical stress.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Temperature stability, not just peak voltage, is the qualification gate for automotive power semis — the differentiator that determines whether GaN wins traction inverter sockets.
insights.quote: Our device can hold high voltage across a wide temperature range, making it suitable for EVs or industrial power systems
insights.locator: Luca Mazzone, a PhD student at EPFL

insights.claim: A Nagoya University, MIT, Cornell, City University of Hong Kong and Chinese Academy of Sciences team achieved p-GaN contact resistivity of (1-3) x 10^-4 ohm-cm^2 by depositing an ultrathin magnesium layer and heating at 600C for five minutes, claimed among the lowest reported for thin p-type GaN.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: p-type contact resistance is the classic bottleneck limiting GaN device efficiency and LED performance; cutting it opens headroom in both power transistors and optoelectronics.
insights.quote: The process achieved a contact resistivity of (1–3) × 10⁻⁴ Ω cm² without damaging the surface, which the team claims is among the lowest reported contact resistivities for thin p-type GaN.

insights.claim: The mechanism is that during soft annealing the ultrathin magnesium is rapidly consumed as it diffuses into the p-GaN surface region, creating an ultrahigh-concentration Mg-doped layer that narrows the contact depletion region and promotes hole tunneling, while leaving a smoother surface than thick Mg layers.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: A tunneling-based contact mechanism reproducible with standard deposition and anneal steps is far more transferable to production than exotic contact schemes.

insights.claim: The team found surprisingly that a protective cap made no difference to magnesium oxidation, with only the very top layer oxidizing even at 10nm thickness, removing the impurity-adding capping step that was assumed necessary.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Eliminating a capping layer removes both cost and a contamination source — the kind of process simplification that decides whether a lab result reaches fabs.
insights.quote: The team tried a capless sample as a reference, and surprisingly found that the cap didn't make a difference, with only the very top layer becoming oxidized even at 10nm thicknesses.

insights.claim: The magnesium contact process is simpler, quicker and cheaper than bottom-up crystal growth and can be applied after device processing, with the team now extending it to LEDs and power transistors for EVs.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Back-end compatibility means existing GaN lines could adopt it without re-qualifying epitaxy — a short path from paper to production for GaN device makers.
insights.quote: The process was also simpler, quicker, and cheaper to implement than bottom-up crystal growth, and can be applied after device processing.

insights.claim: MIT, Georgia Tech and Penn State embedded GaN transistors into an ultrathin single-crystal diamond layer acting as a heat spreader that normalizes temperature, letting the transistors approach peak performance without reducing reliability.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Diamond as an interposer material rather than a coating turns thermal management into an integration-layer product category — watch synthetic diamond substrate suppliers.

insights.claim: MIT's Pradyot Yadav argues that because no single material can do everything well in a wireless device, 3D heterogeneously integrated systems are here to stay, and matching GaN and silicon temperatures via an embedded thermal material improves overall 3D chip reliability.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Frames thermal co-design, not just interconnect, as the reliability gate on heterogeneous integration — a persistent demand driver for advanced thermal materials.
insights.quote: No single material can do everything well in a wireless device, so these 3D heterogeneously integrated systems are here to stay

insights.claim: Putting GaN transistors into a diamond interposer improves device performance rather than degrading it, inverting the usual expectation that heterogeneous integration costs performance.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: If integration is performance-additive rather than a compromise, the economic case for advanced packaging strengthens well beyond density arguments.
insights.quote: By putting these GaN transistors into a diamond interposer, we are actually able to improve the performance of the device, as opposed to degrading it. We can get the best of both worlds.

insights.claim: The fabrication flow cuts GaN dielets from a wafer, drills cavities in single-crystal diamond with a femtosecond laser, seats the dielets on die-attach film under heat and pressure, then stacks dielectric and metal layers on top of GaN and diamond together.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Femtosecond laser machining of diamond becomes a required capability for this class of packaging — a niche equipment demand signal.
insights.locator: The process starts by cutting prepared gallium nitride dielets

insights.claim: The team used the diamond interposer technique to build a power amplifier for wireless communications, framed as the beating heart of a wireless device front end whose performance dictates the entire communication system's performance, and powerful enough to propagate a signal for miles.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: PA performance gates system-level radio economics, so thermal-enabled PA gains translate directly into fewer base stations or longer range per node.
insights.quote: The power amplifier is the beating heart of a wireless device front end. Its performance will dictate the entire performance of your communication system.

insights.claim: Named applications for the diamond-interposer GaN amplifier span high-power radars, space communications, industrial drones and data center power conversion, tying one RF packaging advance to both defense and AI-datacenter demand pools.
insights.speaker: Jesse Allen
insights.so_what: Dual-use exposure across defense RF and datacenter power gives GaN packaging suppliers two independent, currently well-funded demand cycles.
insights.quote: Applications could include high-power radars, space communications, industrial drones, and data center power conversion.
